item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I absolutely adore this article for reasons that are beyond my comprehension. To me, it's absolutely dripping with anomalous paranoia and tension that so many articles based on the Soviet Union possess. I even have a headcanon for many details in the article that dovetail stupidly well with SCP-2664:

"Project [REDACTED], a Soviet [DATA EXPUNGED]."

This is a coverup of Project Redline, a Soviet eigenweapon. The thing that the Soviets were transporting was another baby psychic eigenweapon - an infant powerful enough to make 2664 look like a fortune teller. The baby is still alive inside the submarine - it's treating it as a gigantic womb, a place for it to gestate and mature; and using its abilities unconsciously to influence the environment and sea life to protect it.

"On █████████, SCPS Basisty reported a submerged contact approaching SCP-741 from the south at 46 knots. Acoustic signature of the contact did not match any known submarine or torpedo. Contact did not respond to sonobuoy drops or active sonar pings."

The mystery party that tried to retrieve the thing was Scarlet Hammer, a splinter terrorist faction of GRU Division P.

"They mentioned a covert op by the Soviet military against an internal, unnamed faction, to get rid of "terrifying weapons" that "even the Soviet Union can't safely control"."

This is part of Khrushchev's purge of GRU Division "P" as stated in 2664.

I'd love to write a tale about this at some point in the future to expand upon this headcanon - if anyone else is feeling suitably inspired, I urge you to go for it!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Regarding what exactly the Russians were doing with whatever is aboard the sub: my thinking is that they don't want to dispose of it, not entirely. If they wanted to obliterate whatever is on board, there are safer ways to do so. Place it under the epicentre of a 50-megaton nuclear bomb on Novaya Zemlya (like the protocol for the COLD HARPER object detailed in transcript-of-meeting-june-2-1972), or entomb it at the bottom of the Kola Superdeep Borehole, for example. No, whatever this is, the Russians didn't intend to destroy it, they wanted to preserve it. To put it somewhere where it's inaccessible, but where they can still retrieve it, maybe as an all-powerful Mutually Assured Destruction item, or an extension of the Dead Hand system.

About the retrieval: if you read between the lines and know about Project Azorian, you can work out what happened when the US government tried to salvage it. They snapped it in half due to an equipment failure, and pulled up the bow…except there wasn't anything in it. The claim that six bodies were recovered was a sham. There were plenty of indications that the sub had been fully crewed when it left port, but when the hulk was examined, there was nobody on board, and no sign of where they went. All that was pulled up was a section of the bow (not containing the anomaly, which may in fact be outside of the hull) showing evidence of at least one fired missile, and a single nuclear warhead configured as a demolition device.

I tried to stay away from doing that with the unidentified vessel, including a heavily-redacted followup like that always struck me as something of a cop-out.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Okay, in order…
1: already been covered by Lexagon.
2: I'd imagine the pressure region would be hemispherical, extending 250m as its radius from the centre point.
3: fair point, it could use some explanation, but I'm not entirely sure what to say.
4: ah, you missed the significance of that bit. The partial recovery alludes to Project Azorian (AKA Jennifer), the attempt by the CIA to recover the Soviet submarine K-129 in 1974. The lift using the Glomar Explorer was only partially successful, all they managed to raise was a section of the bow containing two nuclear torpedoes and six dead crewmen. Now, whether or not SCP-741 actually is K-129 is up for debate, although the dates match, K-129 is a Golf-II-class, not a Charlie-II. That's all up to the reader's imagination.
5: hm, that's a decent point
6: yes, definitely. One of the key aspects of submarine warfare is knowing the sounds made by other vessels. Hydrophone arrays can be used to pick up these sounds like was done with the USS Scorpion, and trained operators can interpret them to indicate exactly what's going on.

And regarding the unidentified sub? Just about everything regarding it is weird. The drive's totally unidentified (read that passage more closely, it doesn't match magnetohydrodynamic), those missiles are much too slow to be modern ASMs, not to mention that they lack any active guidance, and the transient sounds generated as it broke up are considered anomalous. The Foundation would definitely have checked it out, but what exactly it is (if they even know) is still highly classified, fitting with the rest of the article.

I've made a few (okay, a fair number) of impovements for grammar and flow, but a couple things are still bugging me… I didn't want to change them because they're content, not grammar or spelling, but can I get opinions on this?

"…it was largely intact at the time that it sank, save for a hole just forward of the sail and another further aft,…"

When last I checked, submarines don't have sails.

"The wreck is surrounded by an anomalous pressure gradient extending approximately 250m centered on a point 30m aft…"

250m radius or diameter? Also, does this pressure gradient have the same vertical [radius? diameter?] as it does horizontal?

"…the submarine had been deployed under unusual circumstances…"

I feel like that needs to be cleared up a bit…

"The United States government attempted to recover the vessel…" "This was moderately successful, though precisely what it recovered was never disclosed."

So… Was it successful in recovering the vessel, or not? If they recovered the vessel, then what they recovered has been disclosed: the vessel. If they didn't recover the vessel (which they obviously didn't, as it's still there), the mission can't be described as having been moderately successful. I think the best way to fix this is to change that first bit to read, "attempted to recover THE CONTENTS OF the vessel".

"Special protection is also required for divers to approach the wreck."

I feel like this should be noted in the Special Containment Procedures in greater detail.

"Afterward, hostile could be heard engaging in evasive maneuvers, followed by four closely-spaced explosions and the sound of a submarine disintegrating."

I honestly just don't know this — WOULD you be able to hear this? Do submarines make particular sounds when they disintegrate? Do submarines make sounds that are audible from the surface when they move about underwater? The explosions I'm sure you could hear, but I'm dubious about the rest.

General complaint about Incident Report I741-C: are you telling me that no-one went under and took a look at the wreckage of the submarine with magnetohydrodynamic drive? I refuse to believe that the Foundation wouldn't've checked that shit out; I mean, come on.

The North Sea is fairly deep - a wrecked sub might be fairly hard to notice. As for the exchange of missiles, it's distantly possible that the Russians (who are the publicly-acknowledged owners of SCPS Tunguska) could pass it off as a live-fire exercise, particularly if only civilian ships were in the area.

Also, the region could be an exclusion zone for some other reason - it might be near where Kursk went down. In real life all Kursk's weapons were recovered, but suppose they weren't, and she did indeed have some nuke-tipped P-700 Granit rounds aboard…
